questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Intercepts of a Normal Line
questions.problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =-\frac{1}{5}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{5}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5} & =0 \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(16,0).$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Equation of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point
questions.problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{5}-2x$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=ax+b$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. Find the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{5}-2x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{5}-2x)=10{x}^{4}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=10(1)^{4}-2=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{8}+\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a+b=-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{8}=0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Equation of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point
questions.problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}$ at the point $(1,4)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $q-p.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =-2{x}^{-3/2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{1}^{3}}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ 2y-8 & =x-1 \\ x-2y & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q-p=-7-(-2)=-5.$

questions.problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{2}{x}+1$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
questions.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{x}+1) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-1}+1) \\  & =-2{x}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{(1)^{2}}=-2,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2}+3 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2} & =0 \\ x & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the  $x$-axis at $(\,-5,0\,).$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=4-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{1}{4},2):$

$$
m={f}^{′}(\frac{1}{4})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{3}}}=4
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{′}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{′} & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
